System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ How a commit works (git internals)
Inside One Commit: snapshots, fingerprints & “sticker magic”

• A commit is the metadata + pointers to content, not a full copy
• “FILES COPIED 0 / COMMITS 0” — Git reuses objects by content identity
• Snapshots: your project state is reconstructed from stored objects
• Fingerprints: content is hashed; the same content maps to the same object
• Branches: cheap refs (tiny pointers), cost ~41 bytes because they don’t duplicate history
• Why it’s fast: immutability + deduplication + object addressing

Practical takeaway: In interviews, describe versioning as “content-addressed DAG snapshots,” not “folders copied per commit.”

Debate question: Should production systems prefer “copy-on-write snapshots” (Git style) or “in-place updates” for performance and reliability?

System Design & Software Architecture Explained ⚡ Today’s deep dive: git internals—what’s actually inside “one commit,” and why it scales.

Under the hood, Git behaves like a content-addressed storage system:

• Commits aren’t full filesystem copies. They’re metadata objects that reference other objects.
• Snapshots are conceptual: the tree you see at HEAD is reconstructed via pointers to stored content objects.
• Fingerprints (hashes) make deduplication natural. If two states share the same content, Git reuses the same objects.
• “Sticker magic”: think of the commit as a sticker that points to an immutable content graph. The sticker changes; the underlying pieces are shared.

Why branches feel “cheap”:

• A branch is essentially a ref (a pointer) to a commit—small and fast to create.
• The history remains a DAG of immutable objects; branching doesn’t require duplicating the underlying content.
• This is the same architectural idea behind scalable systems: avoid copying large state; reference immutable artifacts.

Trade-offs / production lessons:

• Immutable objects simplify concurrency and auditing—great for reliable rebuilds.
• Hash-addressing improves integrity and caching opportunities.
• Garbage collection becomes an operational concern: you manage object lifetimes, not just logical history.

Interview tip: When asked about “version control internals,” answer with: “content-addressed immutable objects + commit/tree pointers = a DAG of snapshots,” then connect it to real systems (CAS, immutability, caching).
